verdict.rationale: Both changes swap the quadratic findIndex scan for a normalized-email Map that keeps the first index, so behavior is the same and the speedup is equivalent. B adds a wall-clock performance test with a 1-second threshold, which can fail randomly on slow CI machines. A deliberately left such a test out and instead benchmarked old against new, confirming identical output. B's main loop is slightly more readable than A's `remember(contact.email, result.push(contact) - 1)`, but the flaky test and A's stronger verification tip it to A.
a_issues: `remember(contact.email, result.push(contact) - 1)` is terse and re-normalizes an email that was already normalized for the lookup
Benchmark script was deleted, so the speedup is not reproducible from the repo
b_issues: Added a wall-clock timing test (<1000ms) that may fail randomly on slow or loaded CI machines
Did not time the old version, so the report's 'minutes to milliseconds' claim is partly inferred
Introduces a separate helper function for a two-line check that is used only once

verdict.rationale: Both changes make the same correct fix: a Map from normalized email to the first index, updated as contacts are appended. Behaviour is preserved in both, including first-entry-wins for duplicates in the stored book. B's report is better grounded: it measured old against new (67 s to 38 ms with identical output) and confirmed its new test against the old code. A did not time the old version and added a wall-clock test that could fail randomly on slow machines. A's code reads slightly more cleanly, but B's verification and test choices tip the balance.
a_issues: Adds a wall-clock timing assertion (< 1s) to the unit suite, which can fail randomly on slow or loaded CI machines.
The report claims 'milliseconds instead of minutes' without having timed the old version.
The repeated-email test checks only the tags array, not which entry ids received the merge, so it is less explicit.
b_issues: `remember` normalizes the incoming email a second time after the lookup already did. This is redundant, though cheap.
`result.push(contact) - 1` is a slightly clever idiom and is less obvious than using `result.length` before pushing.
No test in the suite guards against a return to quadratic behaviour; only a deleted ad-hoc benchmark covered it.
